title.text:
Ship it: reproducible work, a
small app and responsible use

objects.text: How do we turn a notebook into something a colleague can repeat, use and trust?

AI and Data Science Professional  |  Session 23 of 24  |  Module F: Ship it and present
KLAi Professional Learning  |  Jotham Martin Wambi

slides.notes: Welcome back. For twenty-two sessions your work has lived in a notebook that only you could run. Today it leaves the notebook. You will make it repeatable, save the model, put the code on GitHub, and see how a small app is built. Then comes the part that decides whether anyone should use it: a model card, a watch for drift, a fairness audit by group and the duties under Uganda law.

slides.notes:
Here is what you can do by the end of today. You can make a notebook reproducible, which means a colleague gets your result, and you can save a trained model to a file and publish code and a small app for free. You can write a model card, and you can watch for data drift and concept drift.

And you can run a fairness audit by group, spot a proxy variable, and name the main duties in the Uganda Data Protection and Privacy Act of 2019. The lab uses the Nile Microfinance loans, and it ends with a folder you can keep and show.

title.text:
Your two hours: concepts
first, then a notebook lab

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/x_plan_11.90x2.95_83d54561.png
objects.alt: The two hours in parts, in minutes

objects.text: Ideas with pictures first. Then you open the notebook. Then the checks and what you keep.

slides.notes:
We have two hours. The first ten minutes bring back Session 22 and set the question for today. Then forty-five minutes of concepts with no laptops open: how to make work repeatable, how to save and share it, and how to check it is fair and lawful. After a ten minute break we open one Colab notebook for a forty-five minute lab on the Nile Microfinance loans.

The last ten minutes are an exit check and what you keep. Please protect the lab time, because the fairness checks only make sense when you run them.

title.text: Three questions from last time

runs.text: 1.  A language model states a fact that is in none of your documents. What is that called, and what did we add to reduce it?
2.  Why do we keep an evaluation set of test questions for a document assistant?
3.  What is a chunk?

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/icon_question_2.80.png

objects.text: Answer aloud first. Then we check together.

slides.notes:
Three quick questions from Session 22. Answer aloud first, and then we check together. It is a warm-up to bring last time back.

Question one. A language model states a fact that is in none of your documents. What is that called, and what did we add to reduce it?

A good answer is this. A hallucination: fluent text that is invented. Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) finds passages in your own documents first and answers from them.

Question two. Why do we keep an evaluation set of test questions for a document assistant?

A good answer is this. So we can run the same questions after every change and see whether the answers got better or worse.

Question three. What is a chunk?

A good answer is this. A piece of a document, such as one paragraph of a policy, that is stored and searched on its own.

If you missed one, check your notes from last session tonight. Now to today.

slides.notes:
Here are the answers to the three warm-up questions. A fact that appears in none of your documents is a hallucination: fluent text that is invented. Retrieval-augmented generation, or RAG, reduces it by finding passages in your own documents first. An evaluation set is a list of test questions with checked answers, so you can run it again after every change.

And a chunk is a piece of a document that is stored and searched on its own. Today is about the same habit of repeating and checking, applied to everything you ship. Which of the three was hardest?

title.text: Words we use today

rows.text: A colleague who runs your notebook gets your result. It needs a fixed random seed, recorded library versions and a run from the top.
Saving a trained model to a file, for example with joblib or pickle, so it can be loaded later without training again.
Data drift: the inputs change after training. Concept drift: the link between the inputs and the outcome changes.
Compare approval and error rates across groups. A proxy variable stands in for a column you left out. Disparate impact is the ratio of two approval rates.
Information that identifies a person. The person is the data subject. The organisation that decides how it is used is the data controller.

/sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/icon_people_0.70.png

slides.notes:
Five words for today. I give the plain meaning of each, and we use every one of them before the end of the session.

Reproducibility. A colleague who runs your notebook gets your result. It needs a fixed random seed, recorded library versions and a run from the top.

Model serialisation (persistence). Saving a trained model to a file, for example with joblib or pickle, so it can be loaded later without training again.

Data drift (and concept drift). Data drift: the inputs change after training. Concept drift: the link between the inputs and the outcome changes.

Fairness audit (proxy variable, disparate impact). Compare approval and error rates across groups. A proxy variable stands in for a column you left out. Disparate impact is the ratio of two approval rates.

Personal data (data subject, data controller). Information that identifies a person. The person is the data subject. The organisation that decides how it is used is the data controller.

title.text:
Shipping a model means five
jobs after the notebook works

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/x_flow_11.90x3.90_6f2f8381.png
objects.alt: Shipping a model means five jobs after the notebook works

objects.text: Today covers all five. The lab does 1 and 2, writes the files for 4, and does 5. You do 3 and the deployment with your own free accounts.

slides.notes:
A notebook that works for you is only the start. Five jobs follow. First, make it repeatable with a seed, recorded library versions and a clean run from the top. Second, save the trained model as a file. Third, share the code with Git and GitHub. Fourth, serve the model through a small web app built with Streamlit.

And fifth, govern it: write a model card, watch for drift, audit it for fairness by group and check your duties under the law. The first four are craft. The fifth decides whether anyone should trust the other four. Which job do you skip most often today?

title.text: A random seed makes a random draw repeatable

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/x_dl_runs_7.70x4.80_60b90f40.png
objects.alt: A random seed makes a random draw repeatable

objects.text: Seed (random_state): a starting number for the random generator. The same seed gives the same draw.

runs.text: In pandas: random_state=42.
In Sheets, paste RAND as values.
Use one seed for every random split.

slides.notes:
Many steps in data science use chance: drawing a sample, splitting training and test sets, starting a model. If chance changes every run, nobody can repeat your result. A random seed fixes it. It is a starting number for the random generator. Look at the picture. Drawing five loans with seed forty-two gives the same five row numbers twice.

Seed forty-three gives a different draw, but again the same twice. In a spreadsheet the same problem exists with RAND, which changes every time the sheet recalculates, and you freeze it by pasting the values. Which random steps have you used so far in this course?

title.text:
A requirements file records which
library versions your notebook used

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/x_dl_file_7.70x4.80_84f59556.png
objects.alt: A requirements file records which library versions your notebook used

objects.text: Requirements file (requirements.txt): a text file that lists each library and its version.

runs.text: The versions shown come from one machine. Print your own: numpy.__version__, or pip freeze.
Keep only libraries you import.
Install with pip install -r requirements.txt.

slides.notes:
Libraries change over time, and a notebook that works with one version can fail or give different numbers with another. So you record the versions. In Python every library prints its version, for example numpy is 2.2.6 and pandas is 2.3.3 on the machine that built this slide.

Your own versions will differ, and that is fine. You list the libraries you import in a plain text file called requirements dot txt, one per line, with the version after two equals signs. A colleague, or a deployment service, installs exactly those. Which libraries would your course project notebook need?

title.text: Restart and run all is the test of a notebook

objects.text: Works only for you

runs.text: You ran cells in a different order.
Your open session remembers a deleted cell.
A colleague meets a NameError.

objects.text: Works for anyone

runs.text: Runtime, then Restart session and run all.
Fix the first error and run again.
Share when it runs top to bottom.

objects.text: Run it from the top before you share it.

slides.notes:
The third habit is the order. While you work you run cells in any order, and your open session remembers every name you ever created, even from a cell you deleted. Your colleague opens the notebook with an empty session and runs it from the top. If a cell depends on something that is no longer there, they meet an error that says a name is not defined.

The test is simple. In Colab choose Runtime, then Restart session and run all. Fix the first error, then run again. Only share a notebook that runs from top to bottom by itself. Has this ever happened to you?

title.text:
Model serialisation saves a trained
model to a file you can load later

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/x_flow_7.70x4.80_2f9ff02b.png
objects.alt: Model serialisation saves a trained model to a file you can load later

objects.text: Model serialisation (persistence): saving a trained model to a file.

runs.text: Tools: joblib or pickle. joblib uses pickle underneath.
Load only files you trust: loading can run hidden code.
Use the same library versions.

slides.notes:
Training a model takes effort, so you save the result. Model serialisation, also called persistence, writes the trained model to a file. In Python the common tool for scikit-learn models is joblib, and the standard Python tool is pickle. Joblib uses pickle underneath, so it carries the same risk.

The picture shows three steps: train, save with dump, and load with load, then predict. Two warnings. My understanding from the library documentation is that loading a file can run code that is inside it, so never load a model file from a stranger. And save and load with the same library versions, or you may get warnings or wrong results.

Where would you store a model file at work?

title.text:
Git keeps a history of your project,
and GitHub keeps a copy online

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/x_dl_git_11.90x4.25_a6191bca.png
objects.alt: Git keeps a history of your project, and GitHub keeps a copy online

objects.text: Git is the tool on your laptop. GitHub hosts a copy online.

slides.notes:
Git is a tool that keeps the history of a project folder. The folder you edit is the working folder. With git add you choose which changed files go into the next saved version. With git commit you save that version in your local repository, together with a short message saying what changed.

And with git push you upload your commits to GitHub, a website that hosts a copy so colleagues can see it. In Google Drive you have version history. Git is the same idea, but you choose when to save a version and you name it. What would your commit messages say?

title.text: Six words you will hear about Git and GitHub

rows.text: The project folder together with its full history.
One saved version, with a message saying what changed.
A separate line of work. The main line is called main.
The front page of a repository: what the project is and how to run it.
A list of files Git must never track, such as data with personal details or passwords.

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/icon_folder_0.50.png
/sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/icon_check_0.50.png
/sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/icon_pin_0.50.png
/sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/icon_cloud_0.36.png
/sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/icon_doc_0.50.png
/sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/icon_lock_0.50.png

slides.notes:
Six words you will meet the first day you use GitHub. A repository, or repo, is the project folder together with its history. A commit is one saved version with a message. A branch is a separate line of work, and the main line is called main. Push means uploading your commits to GitHub.

A README is the front page of the repository: what the project is and how to run it. And a dot gitignore file lists files Git must never track, such as data with personal details or passwords. Which of these would you create first?

title.text:
A public repository is public: personal
data, passwords and keys never go in

objects.text: Put in

runs.text: The notebook, run from the top.
app.py and requirements.txt.
A README and the model card.
Generated or public data.

objects.text: Never put in

runs.text: Names, phones or loan records of real people.
Passwords, keys and tokens.
Data your employer has not cleared.

objects.text: Deleting a file later does not erase its history. Check before you push.

slides.notes:
Anyone on the internet can read a public repository and copy it. So decide what goes in before the first push. The notebook, the app file, the requirements file, a README and the model card all belong. Data should be generated or public. Never put in personal data such as names, phone numbers or the loan records of real people, and never passwords, keys or tokens, and never data your employer has not agreed to share.

Remember that Git keeps history, so deleting a file in a later commit does not remove it from the earlier ones. A private repository exists, but check the current terms. What would you check in your own folder?

title.text:
A Streamlit app turns a
saved model into a web page

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/x_dl_app_7.70x4.80_813dc8c4.png
objects.alt: A Streamlit app turns a saved model into a web page

objects.text: Streamlit: a free Python library that builds a web page from a script.

runs.text: You write inputs and output. Streamlit draws the page.
These inputs give 14% chance of default.
A person makes the decision.

slides.notes:
Here is what a small app looks like. A person types an income and a loan amount, moves two sliders, and presses a button. The page shows the predicted chance of default, which is 14 percent for these inputs, computed from the same model you will save in the lab.

Streamlit is a free Python library that builds this page from a script. You describe the inputs and the output, and it does the web work. Notice the caption: this is a teaching model on fictional data, and a person decides. Who at your workplace would use an app like this?

title.text:
The whole app is about 25 lines: load
the model, ask for four inputs, predict

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/x_dl_code2_11.90x4.25_840b80e9.png
objects.alt: The whole app is about 25 lines: load the model, ask for four inputs, predict

objects.text: Gold lines: load the model (line 5) and predict (line 24).

slides.notes:
This is the whole app. Lines one to three import the libraries. Line five loads the saved model. Lines seven and eight give the page a title and a caption. Lines ten to fifteen create four inputs: two number boxes and two sliders. Lines seventeen to twenty-one put the four values into a one-row table with the same column names the model was trained on.

Then lines twenty-three to twenty-five add a button which, when pressed, calls predict probability and shows the result. Streamlit runs the script again from the top whenever someone changes an input. Which line would you change first to show a different title?

title.text:
Streamlit Community Cloud can deploy
your app from a GitHub repository

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/x_flow_11.90x3.90_b4832467.png
objects.alt: Streamlit Community Cloud can deploy your app from a GitHub repository

objects.text: Deploy: put the app on a server. Free at the time of writing, with limits on resources and sleeping apps. Check current terms, including private repositories.

slides.notes:
To deploy means to put the app on a server so that other people can open it with a web address. Streamlit Community Cloud can do this for free from a GitHub repository. You need a repository with app dot py, the model file and requirements dot txt.

You sign in with your GitHub account, create a new app, choose the repository, the branch main and the file, and press deploy. It installs the libraries and gives you an address. At the time of writing it is free for public repositories and apps may go to sleep when nobody uses them, with reports of about twelve hours.

Limits change, so check the current terms. It suits learning and demonstrations. A business-critical service needs something stronger. What would you use it for?

title.text:
A model card is a one-page note on
what a model is for and where it can fail

rows.text: Ranks loan applications so an officer knows which to review first. It does not approve or refuse.
8,000 fictional loans, 2023-01 to 2025-09. collection_calls was removed because it leaks the answer.
Simplified four-variable model. AUC 0.727 on 2,000 held-out loans. At decision threshold 0.15 it flags 28% of loans and finds 59% of defaults.
Fictional data. 379 loans lack income and are filled with the median. Four variables only. Not tested after the data changes.
On the held-out loans, approval women 72.3%, men 71.6%. Reviewed by the credit manager and the data protection officer.

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/icon_doc_0.50.png
/sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/icon_folder_0.50.png
/sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/icon_chart_0.50.png
/sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/icon_cross_0.50.png
/sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/icon_shield_0.50.png

objects.text: Update the card every time the model changes.

slides.notes:
A model card is a short note, usually one page, that travels with a model. It says what the model is for, what data it learned from, how well it works, where it can fail, and who reviews it. This card is for the loan model you will build.

The purpose is to rank applications for an officer. It makes no decision. The data is 8,000 fictional loans, with the leaking column removed. This is a simplified model with four variables, fitted on the six thousand training loans. On the 2,000 held-out loans it has never seen, the area under the curve is 0.727, and at a decision threshold of 0.15 it flags 28 percent of loans and finds 59 percent of defaults.

The limits and the fairness check complete it. Which section would your manager read first?

title.text:
Data drift: when new data stops looking
like the training data, the model gets worse

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/x_dl_drift_11.90x4.25_4cc5bd93.png
objects.alt: Data drift: when new data stops looking like the training data, the model gets worse

objects.text: Solid: real. Dashed: a hypothetical 15 percent fall from month 25.

slides.notes:
Data drift means the inputs change after the model was trained. The solid line is real: the mean monthly income of new loans in each month. For the first twenty-four months, the training period, it averages 716 thousand shillings, and in the next nine months 717. So our real data shows no drift.

The dashed line is hypothetical: the same months, but with incomes fifteen percent lower, which would average 610. A model trained on the old picture would now see borrowers it has never met. You catch it by comparing each month of new inputs with the training period. What other input could drift in your data?

title.text: Data drift and concept drift are different problems

objects.text: Data drift

runs.text: The inputs change: incomes or loan sizes move.
Check: compare each month of inputs with the training period.

objects.text: Concept drift

runs.text: The link between inputs and outcome changes. Illustration: a new repayment option changes the risk.
Check: compare predicted with actual defaults.

objects.text: Plan monitoring, set a review date, retrain when needed.

slides.notes:
There are two kinds of drift. In data drift the inputs change, so new borrowers look different from the ones the model learned from. You catch it by comparing summaries of each month of inputs with the training period. In concept drift the relationship between inputs and outcome changes.

As an illustration, suppose a new repayment option changes how borrowers with a given income behave. The inputs look the same but the risk has moved. You catch that only when real outcomes arrive, by comparing predicted with actual defaults. In both cases the answer is a monitoring plan, a review date and retraining on newer data.

When would your outcomes arrive?

title.text:
A proxy variable carries the
information of a column you removed

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/x_dl_groupbars_7.70x4.80_90226f13.png
objects.alt: A proxy variable carries the information of a column you removed

objects.text: Proxy variable: a variable that stands in for another. Occupation stands in for gender.

runs.text: Women are 77% of tailors and 73% of salon owners.
Dropping the gender column keeps the information.
Occupation rules can treat men and women differently.

slides.notes:
Suppose you remove the gender column so the model cannot use it. Fairness is not solved, because other columns can stand in for it. A variable that stands in for another is a proxy variable. The bars show the share of women among 7,621 loans with a known income, by occupation.

Women are 77 percent of tailors and 73 percent of salon owners, and under half of farmers. So a rule that treats occupations differently will treat men and women differently, even though it never sees gender. Which column in your own data might be a proxy?

title.text:
Disparate impact: divide the lower
approval rate by the higher one

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/x_math_11.90x2.25_61edc924.png
objects.alt: Disparate impact: divide the lower approval rate by the higher one

rows.text: Share of a group not flagged as high risk.
Disparate impact ratio. 1.00 means equal rates.
Below 0.8 is a warning. It comes from US employment practice and is no Ugandan legal test.

objects.text: A screening number: it starts a question.

slides.notes:
Here is how to measure unequal treatment. The approval rate of a group is the share of its loans that are not flagged as high risk. Disparate impact compares two groups: divide the lower approval rate by the higher one. A ratio of one means equal rates. For the occupation rule, men are approved 52.4 percent of the time and women 70.3 percent, so the ratio is 0.745.

A common rule of thumb, used in United States employment practice, treats a ratio below zero point eight as a warning. It is not a Ugandan legal test and it is only a prompt to investigate. What would you ask next?

objects.text: Fairness audit: compare approval and error rates across groups.

runs.text: Approval rate: share of loans not flagged.
The occupation rule favours women.
The other two treat groups alike.

slides.notes:
Now the fairness audit. We take three ways to flag a loan as high risk and compute the approval rate for women and men. These are the 2,000 held-out loans that have an income. Rule one flags an instalment-to-income ratio above zero point four, which is about thirty-five percent of income before the illustrative fifteen percent charge: women 65.1 percent, men 64.0.

Rule two flags occupations whose default rate on the training loans is above twelve percent: women 70.3, men 52.4, a ratio of 0.745. The model at a threshold of 0.15 gives 72.3 and 71.6. None of them uses gender, yet one raises a flag. That is the point of auditing the output rather than trusting the inputs.

Which group would you check first at work?

rule misses more defaults among women

objects.text: False negative rate: share of actual defaults the rule did not flag. False positive rate: share of repaid loans it flagged.

slides.notes:
Approval rates are one side. Error rates are the other. A false negative is a default the rule did not flag. A false positive is a repaid loan the rule flagged. The instalment rule makes errors of a similar size for women and men. The occupation rule does not.

It misses 65.7 percent of defaults among women and 42.3 percent among men, and it flags 46.1 percent of repaid loans among men against 29.1 percent among women. So women who will default are missed more often, and men who will repay are flagged more often. Both are harms, to the lender and to the borrower.

Which error costs more at your workplace?

slides.notes:
Now the law. This is a teaching summary in plain words from public descriptions of the Act, and it is not legal advice. Personal data is information from which a person can be identified, such as a name, a phone number or a loan record. The person it describes is the data subject, here the borrower.

The organisation that decides why and how the data is used is the data controller, here the lender. A data processor handles data on the controller behalf, for example a cloud provider. My understanding is that the regulator is the Personal Data Protection Office under NITA-U. For your own case, ask your data protection officer or a lawyer.

Who is the data controller where you work?

slides.notes:
Public summaries of the Act describe seven principles. Accountability: someone is responsible and can show what was done. Fair and lawful processing. Collect only adequate and relevant data, which means only what the purpose needs. Keep data only as long as needed. Keep it accurate. Be open: tell people what you hold and why.

And protect it from loss, leaks and misuse. For a model team, that translates into jobs: write down the purpose on the model card, drop columns you do not need, and never publish personal data. This is a summary, so read the Act itself for the exact words.

Which principle does your current project test most?

slides.notes:
Public summaries list rights for data subjects. Access: asking what data an organisation holds about you. Correction: asking for wrong data to be fixed. Erasure: asking for data to be deleted, in the cases the law allows. And a right related to automated decisions: asking not to be subject to a decision taken only by a computer.

For a model team each right becomes a job: record what data feeds the model, correct and retrain, delete copies, and keep a person who reviews the output. One more row: my understanding is that the Act expects a lawful basis such as consent, and that sending personal data to a server outside Uganda may need extra safeguards, so check before you put real personal data into Colab, GitHub or an app host.

Ask your data protection officer. Which of these would be hardest in your organisation?
